### Environmental setup 
You need to have the `datasets`, `tidyr`, `dplyr`, `rvest`, `stringr`, `lubridate`, `tidytext`, `textdata`, `readr`, `janeaustenr`, and `ggplot2` packages installed. If not yet, please run `install.packages(c("datasets", "tidyr", "dplyr", "rvest", "stringr", "lubridate", "tidytext", "textdata", "readr", "janeaustenr", "ggplot2"))` in your R environment.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
# Load the package.
library(datasets)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(rvest)
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)
library(janeaustenr)
library(tidytext)
library(textdata)
library(ggplot2)
```

### 2. (2 points) Perform different types of joins between the following `employees` and `payroll` data frames using the `"emp_id"` column. Use `left_join`, `right_join`, `inner_join`, and `full_join` to create four resulting data frames, name them appropriately. Display the data frame that contains the most rows.
```{r}
employees <- data.frame(
  emp_id = c(101,102,103,104,105),
  name   = c("Ana","Ben","Chen","Divya","Evan"),
  dept   = c("Data","Data","HR","Finance","Ops")
)
payroll <- data.frame(
  emp_id = c(101,101,102,103,103,103,106),
  month = c(1,2,1,1,2,3,1),
  salary = c(95,100,88,76,80,82,70)
)

```

### 3. (6 points) Use the `rvest` package to scrape the titles, ratings, and prices of books from https://books.toscrape.com/ (the 20 entries on the first page). Store the scraped data in a data frame named `books` and display the top 5 entries ranked by price (highest to lowest). Refer to this tutorial to learn more about HTML scraping: https://r4ds.hadley.nz/webscraping.html.
```{r}
url <- "https://books.toscrape.com/"

```

### 4. (6 points) Extract entries from the following texts using regular expression:

#### a. (2 points) Extract all dates formatted as YYYY-MM-DD or DD/MM/YYYY from the following text: "The event starts on 2026-05-12 and ends on 15/05/2026, with early registration opening on 2026-04-01."
```{r}
text <- "The event starts on 2026-05-12 and ends on 15/05/2026, with early registration opening on 2026-04-01."

```

#### b. (2 points) Extract all full website URLs starting with http:// or https:// from the following text: "Visit our portal at https://www.example.com/home or read docs at http://api.test.org/v2". We assume here that URLs only contain alphabetic and numerical characterers, dots, and slash symbols.
```{r}
text <- "Visit our portal at https://www.example.com/home or read docs at http://api.test.org/v2"

```

#### c. (2 points) Extract all valid 6-character hex color codes (including the leading # symbol) from the following text: "Use #FFFFFF for white background, #333 as shorthand, #00FF00 for success status, and #a1b2c3 for borders." Note that here "#333" should not be matched, only 6-character color codes should be retrieved.
```{r}
text <- "Use #FFFFFF for white background, #333 as shorthand, #00FF00 for success status, and #a1b2c3 for borders."

```

### 6. (20 points) Explore text mining and sentiment analysis across Jane Austen's works, and answer the following questions.

#### a. (2 points) Load the `austen_books()` dataset from the `janeaustenr` package as `books`. Print the dimensions (rows and columns) of `books`, the unique book titles contained in the dataset, and display the first 5 rows.

```{r}

```

#### b. (2 points) Identify the total line count for each book in `books`. Sort the books in descending order by line count, and show the five longest books. Store them in a separate data frame named `long_books`
```{r}

```

#### c. (2 points) For each book in `long_books`, find the line that contains the maximum number of characters. If there are ties, keep the line that appears earliest in the text. Display these resulting lines in a new data frame. (Hint: use `row_number` for numbering lines, use `slice`, `slice_min`, or `slice_max` to select rows.)

```{r}

```

#### d. (2 points) Look at the novel Pride & Prejudice. Extract its content, remove all blank lines containing only whitespace or no characters, and add a sequential line number column "line_id", and print lines 100 to 120 of texts.

```{r}

```

#### e. (3 points) Perform sentiment analysis on the novel Pride & Prejudice. Use the sentiment lexicon `afinn` through `get_sentiments()` using the `textdata` package, save it as a data frame named `word_sentiments`. Tokenize `texts` of your book of interest into words, remove stop words and numbers, and then map the words to `word_sentiments` using an appropriate join function. You only need to keep words that have corresponding sentiments in `afinn`. Count the occurrences of `word` and their corresponding sentiment `value`, sort the results in a descending order according to the occurrence count (`n`) column. What are the ten most frequent words and what are their sentiment values? 
```{r}

```

#### f. (4 points) Analyze the sentiment progression throughout the novel. Calculate the average sentiment score for each line using `word_sentiments`. In this case, do not discard words that have no corresponding sentiment, assign a neutral score of 0. Plot the progression of sentiment versus line number across the novel using an appropriate graph.
```{r}

```

#### g. (5 points) A single line of text can yield a very noisy sentiment signal. Group lines in the novel into segments of `k` lines each, calculate the average sentiment score and plot it in the same type of graph. Be careful that the scale of the axis representing line number shouldn't be changed. Try alter `k` (from 10 to 1000) to generate multiple plots, discuss your findings.

```{r}

```
